papers.title: Rise and Fall of a Superbug: Analyzing the epidemic success of a distinct clone of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium ST117/CT71 in Germany, 2017 - 2024.
papers.abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a major cause of healthcare-associated infections, yet outbreak analysis remains challenging, particularly for prevalent lineages. One of the most striking examples is the Sequence Type (ST) 117/Complex Type (CT) 71/vanB lineage, whose rapid expansion across Germany coincided with a sharp rise in VRE prevalence observed around 2019. Defining reliable genomic thresholds remains particularly difficult, as current core-genome Multi-Locus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) cutoffs are based largely on expert consensus or limited case series. Here, we evaluate the discriminatory performance of cgMLST and split k-mer analysis (SKA) for resolving relatedness within ST117/CT71 and investigate whether low core-genome diversity represents a lineage-specific trait or a population-wide property of E. faecium. While cgMLST captures the overall population structure of ST117/CT71, SKA provided higher resolution, distinguishing isolates identical by cgMLST. Analysis of 2,505 genomes showed that ST117/CT71 does not exhibit reduced allelic variability compared with other hospital-adapted lineages, suggesting that limited core-genome diversity is a broader population characteristic. Complementary transposon analyses further identified two temporally distinct ST117/CT71 sublineages carrying different Tn1549-like structures. To assess allelic variation within confirmed transmission events, we analyzed 138 outbreak clusters from 96 hospitals. Outbreak-associated isolates showed sharply compressed allelic differences (median = 1), with 90% of pairwise comparisons falling within [≤]9 alleles. Thus, the commonly applied [≤]20-allele threshold risks overestimating genomic relatedness and grouping unrelated isolates. Based on these data, we propose lowering the cgMLST alert threshold to [≤]9 alleles for initial cluster detection of local outbreaks, followed by confirmatory high-resolution analyses such as SKA.

papers.title: Saturation barcoding of ribosomal DNA resolves the nucleolar organizer regions of the human genome
papers.abstract: The nucleolus is the hub for ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotic cells. It is assembled on nucleolar organizer regions (NORs), tandem arrays of ribosomal DNA (rDNA) units. In humans, each rDNA unit is ~45 kb and encodes the 47S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) precursor. Hundreds of rDNA units are present per germline genome, spread across 10 NORs positioned on the short arms of the five acrocentric chromosomes. However, their precise count and structure are unknown. In fact, twenty-five years after the first draft of the human genome, NORs are the only regions of the human genome that remain incompletely resolved, represented in telomere-to-telomere (T2T) reference genomes as gaps or modeled sequences rather than bona fide assemblies. Here we use prime editing to insert degenerate 6-bp DNA barcodes to 99% of taggable rDNA units in a clonal derivative of the leukemia-derived K562 cell line. Following ultra-long-read sequencing, these barcodes serve as molecular identifiers that guide the end-to-end assembly of all 18 NORs of K562s pseudotriploid genome. The assembly yields: (i) a precise rDNA copy number for each NOR (range 5-43; total 290); (ii) the cis- and trans- architecture of intragenomic variation in rDNA sequence, both structural and fine-scale; and (iii) patterns of divergence and homogenization within and across NORs that may have arisen during cancer evolution and the subsequent passaging of this line. Finally, by reading the same tags from RNA, we define the relationship between DNA methylation and Pol I transcription at the resolution of individual rDNA units. Together, our study demonstrates how the final tangles of the human genome can at last be resolved, and opens the door to more extensive investigations of how genetic, epigenetic and functional rDNA variation contributes to health and disease.

papers.title: The chromosome-scale genome of the drought-adapted Caatinga tree Spondias tuberosa reveals a conserved, unduplicated architecture within Anacardiaceae
papers.abstract: Spondias tuberosa (umbu) is a tree endemic to the semi-arid Caatinga of north-eastern Brazil, adapted to recurrent drought and high temperatures. Although genomes of mango (Mangifera indica), pistachio (Pistacia vera) and cashew (Anacardium occidentale) are available, comparative analyses of genome evolution across Anacardiaceae remain scarce. We aimed to generate a chromosome-scale reference genome for S. tuberosa and use it to examine genome architecture, meiotic recombination and gene family evolution within the family. We assembled the genome of a single individual using PacBio HiFi and Omni-C (Hi-C) data, mapped meiotic crossovers by single-nucleus RNA sequencing of pollen, and compared the genome with those of six other Sapindales species through orthology, synteny, synonymous substitution (Ks) and gene family expansion/contraction analyses within a dated phylogenomic framework. The assembly anchors 288 Mb onto 16 chromosomes (98.8% BUSCO completeness) and contains 24,232 protein-coding genes, 52.01% repetitive DNA and 1.78 million heterozygous SNPs (0.62%). We identified 1,740 crossovers in 153 pollen nuclei (4.01 cM.Mb1), which were depleted in repeat-rich pericentromeric regions. Ks analyses revealed a whole-genome duplication shared by Mangifera and Anacardium that is absent from S. tuberosa, which retains only the ancient {gamma} triplication. The 97 gene families expanded in S. tuberosa, mostly through tandem duplication, include receptor-like kinases, glutathione S-transferases and disease-resistance proteins, consistent with roles in environmental sensing and stress tolerance. Genome structure has remained highly conserved across Sapindales, except in the mango cashew lineage, which underwent extensive rearrangements following a whole-genome duplication. As sister to the remaining Anacardiaceae sampled and with an unduplicated, largely collinear architecture, S. tuberosa provides a reference for comparative mapping and for transferring genomic information to economically important woody relatives.

papers.title: Single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing reveals isoform usage shifts in mouse acute kidney injury
papers.abstract: Introduction Single-cell and single-nucleus short-read RNA sequencing has elucidated transcriptomic changes across kidney cell types at the gene expression level. However, its limited read length precludes reliable isoform identification, hindering the characterization of individual protein-coding isoforms and non-protein-coding isoforms. We combined long-read sequencing with single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing technologies to investigate isoform regulation in healthy and acutely injured mouse kidneys. Methods Single-cell and single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing datasets were generated from kidneys of three healthy adult male C57BL/6J mice. An additional three adult male C57BL/6J mice underwent bilateral renal ischemia-reperfusion injury, and kidneys were subjected to single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing. Results A total of 1.3 billion reads were generated, with a median read length of 757-884 bases across samples. Single-nucleus libraries yielded a smaller proportion of reads assigned to isoforms than single-cell libraries, reflecting their larger proportion of intronic reads. Nevertheless, single-nucleus libraries detected more distinct isoforms and greater isoform expression diversity, partly owing to the near absence of mitochondrial gene-derived transcripts. Single-nucleus analysis of healthy and injured kidneys revealed that ischemia-reperfusion injury downregulated oxidative phosphorylation-associated genes in proximal tubule cells both at the gene expression level and through shifts in isoform composition. Beyond oxidative phosphorylation-associated genes, Fut9 and Prrc2b were identified as genes exhibiting prominent shifts in isoform usage after ischemia-reperfusion injury. Conclusion Single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing detected injury-induced shifts in isoform usage in mouse kidney, adding a layer of transcriptomic information that is largely inaccessible to conventional gene-level short-read analysis.

papers.title: Long-read analysis of complete human 5S rDNA arrays reveals a zoned organization with two-state unit methylation linked to chromatin architecture
papers.abstract: Despite the fundamental importance of the 5S ribosomal DNA (rDNA) to all cellular life, the landscape of its units by position along its array has remained poorly understood. Here, recent telomere-to-telomere long-read sequencing is used to resolve 5S rDNA arrays from flank to flank and to follow the state of each unit along single molecules. The array is zoned at both the sequence and the epigenetic level. Notably, methylation is bimodal at the level of the unit, and the combination of low-methylation and high-methylation units gives rise to the overall methylation pattern of the array. Moreover, the average number of low-methylation units remains relatively constant regardless of array length. Chromatin fiber sequencing (Fiber-seq) data further show that low-methylation units are more accessible, have lower nucleosome occupancy and are more frequently footprinted at the TFIIIB-binding site, consistent with analyses of ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data from cell lines. Across species, this pattern is shared among apes, whereas other species show diverse patterns. These results provide a unit-resolved view of the human 5S rDNA array and reveal a zone-specific organization of unit methylation that is associated with chromatin architecture.

papers.title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of the endangered northern dragonhead sap beetle, Thymogethes norvegicus (Easton, 1959)
papers.abstract: The northern dragonhead sap beetle (Thymogethes norvegicus) is believed to be endemic to Norway and is classified as endangered. Its life cycle is closely tied to the host plant northern dragonhead (Dracocephalum ruyschiana), itself classified as vulnerable in Norway. Here, we present a chromosome-level genome assembly of a male T. norvegicus. The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes, hap1 and hap2, of 1,142 and 1,109 Mb, with 96.3% and 96.8% scaffolded into chromosomes, respectively. Hap1 contains 8 autosomes and the X chromosome, while hap2 contains 8 autosomes. Assembly quality was high, with conserved single-copy ortholog completeness scores of 96.6% and 90.7% and combined k-mer completeness of 98.1%. A total of 13,484 and 12,550 protein-coding genes were annotated in hap1 and hap2, respectively. This assembly provides a valuable genomic resource for the conservation of this endangered endemic species totally dependent on the vulnerable plant, the northern dragonhead.

papers.title: Genome-wide diversity across 130 years reveals drastic post-bottleneck genetic erosion in a recovering population of golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos)
papers.abstract: Many wild populations have experienced severe human-induced declines, but the genetic consequences of such bottlenecks are often poorly understood. In Finland, as well as in many other countries, golden eagles were heavily persecuted during the 19th-20th centuries, disappearing from southern regions and reaching their lowest population size in the 1950-1960s. Although conservation efforts facilitated demographic recovery, the long-term genomic consequences of the bottleneck remained unknown. Here, we used whole-genome sequencing data spanning 136 years to evaluate patterns of genetic diversity in 26 Finnish golden eagles before, during, and after the mid-20th century bottleneck. We found substantial loss of genetic variation, including an 82% reduction in genome-wide heterozygosity, a 42% decline in nucleotide diversity, a 67% reduction in Watterson's theta, and a substantial loss of variable sites. Analyses of the site frequency spectrum and Tajima's D confirmed historical population contraction, and runs of homozygosity analysis indicated elevated post-bottleneck inbreeding. These results indicate strong genetic erosion in Finnish golden eagles despite the census size recovery. Therefore, incorporating genomic indicators in conservation monitoring and performing regional assessments are necessary to guide management and preserve biodiversity in line with the Global Biodiversity Framework's goal of maintaining genetic variation.

papers.title: Non-coding RNA controls long-range enhancer-promoter interactions
papers.abstract: Transcription regulation depends on interactions between enhancers and gene promoters, which often occur over large genomic distances. The molecular drivers of long-range enhancer-promoter interactions remain poorly understood. Enhancers themselves are known to be transcribed into non-coding RNAs, but the function of these transcripts is unclear. Here, we use acute genetic and chemical perturbations of transcription elongation and termination to study the role of non-coding RNA in enhancer-promoter interactions. By integrating high-resolution 3D genome mapping, transcriptomics, proteomics, biochemistry and live-cell super-resolution imaging in these perturbation contexts, we demonstrate that a strong increase in RNA molecules at enhancers disrupts their long-range interactions with gene promoters, whereas decreased RNA levels lead to stabilization of these interactions. Using separation-of-function perturbations, we show that this regulatory function of RNA is independent from the process of transcription and the proteins recruited to initiate transcription. Functionally, we show that RNA-mediated disruption of enhancer-promoter interactions is associated with reduced transcription of target genes, indicating a regulatory feedback mechanism. Together, our results uncover an additional regulatory principle of enhancer-promoter interactions mediated by non-coding RNA.

papers.title: LIGR-Nue for the global mapping of the bacterial sRNA targetome in vivo
papers.abstract: Interactions between regulatory small RNAs (sRNAs) and their target transcripts are central for post-transcriptional regulation in bacteria. Based on RNA-seq analysis, we determined the relative abundance of several sRNAs in the photosynthetic cyanobacterium Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 under photoautotrophic growth conditions and after transfer to darkness. We observed an increase in the abundance of the sRNAs DsiR1 to 58.6% and of CsiR1 to 19% of the sRNA transcriptome after transfer to darkness. We then developed a duplex-directed, transcriptome-wide mapping strategy of RNA-RNA interactions in vivo, called LIGR-Nue, which involves aminomethyltrioxsalen-mediated UV cross-linking, proximity ligation, crosslink reversal, reverse transcription and sequencing. The data were analysed using the RNANUE pipeline for the detection of chimeric reads and mapping, and benchmarked against known targetome data for the sRNAs PsrR1 and NsiR4. Using this methodology, we identified RNA-RNA interactions, such as PsrR1 as a regulator of carbon assimilation, and DsiR1 as a global silencing factor of photosynthesis-associated mRNAs in the dark. This data enables the comprehensive analysis of sRNA functions in post-transcriptional gene regulation. LIGR-Nue is broadly applicable to map RNA-RNA interactions in bacteria.

papers.title: Gene-level structure of prior knowledge and perturbation responses informs target-level predictability in prior-informed models
papers.abstract: Background: Predictive models of transcriptional responses to unseen genetic perturbations increasingly incorporate biological prior knowledge. However, it remains unclear how well prior knowledge reflects each target's perturbation-response relationships and how closely prior-derived measures track target-level predictive performance. Here, we develop a gene-similarity framework to quantify agreement among eight sources of biological prior knowledge and between prior knowledge and co-function or co-regulation relationships derived from six Perturb-seq datasets. Results: In genome-wide and essential-gene screens, prior agreement accounted for 30-47% of the variance in co-function agreement and 35-43% in co-regulation agreement. Agreement with Perturb-seq responses was higher for essential genes, lower for transcription factor and signaling genes, and varied with gene expression characteristics and cellular context. We compared prior agreement and prior-derived train-test similarity with measures based on the observed test response in tracking target-level predictive performance. Across three prior-informed models, predictions were more accurate for targets whose observed perturbation-response relationships better matched prior knowledge and that were more similar to training perturbations. Notably, prior agreement and prior-derived train-test similarity, calculated without the test response, tracked relative differences in target-level predictive performance. The strength of these associations varied across models and datasets and, for train-test similarity, across prior sources. Conclusion: Our framework reveals gene- and context-level heterogeneity in how biological knowledge aligns with perturbation responses, and provides an a priori basis for assessing relative perturbation predictability before perturbation responses are measured.

papers.title: Long-range regulatory sequence models reveal a phylogenetic boundary in vertebrate genome evolution
papers.abstract: Regulatory activity at a locus depends on local sequence and on long-range interactions with sequence further away, but how long each kind of information stays shared between genomes over evolution is unknown. Here we use sequence-to-function models as a comparative assay, training FunFormer, a long-context binary classifier that reads 20 kb, together with an architecture- and parameter-matched control that reads only the central 1 kb, in six vertebrates spanning 435 million years, and measuring what each retains when applied to another genome. Within species, the long-context model outperformed three published 1 kb classifiers by 1.0 to 3.8 percentage points in every genome, a gain that came from context rather than architecture. Across species, its contribution decayed with divergence, was near zero at the amniote split and reversed between 320 and 435 Mya, while local sequence still transferred into fish. Zebrafish and Atlantic salmon, which share their divergence from tetrapods but differ by the salmonid genome duplication, behaved alike, so the reversal is not explained by the salmonid duplication. An in silico flank intervention showed that replacing the flank with GC-matched sequence from the target genome cost 8 percentage points among mammals. When a mammalian model was applied to fish, a flank drawn from the source genome on average performed as well as the target's own flank, so the model drew nothing from the fish flank that an arbitrary source-genome flank did not provide. The long-range information that these models learn therefore stops being shared between vertebrate genomes well before the local information does. The same boundary sets a practical rule for reusing models in species without their own data, where long context helps among close relatives but is a liability across deep splits, and in variant scoring most foreign models matched a native model in data-limited pig but none did in human.

papers.title: Contig-Resolved Genetic Context of Antimicrobial Resistome in Sediments of Two Contrasting Wastewater-Impacted Rivers
papers.abstract: River sediments harbor diverse antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants; however, gene abundance alone provides limited insight into their genomic context, mobility potential, and associated bacterial hosts. This study employed an assembly- and read-mapping metagenomic framework to surface-sediment metagenomes (40.78 Gb clean data) from two contrasting wastewater-impacted Indian rivers, Adyar (Chennai) and Musi (Hyderabad), retaining sample-, contig- and open reading frame level provenance. ARG-carrying contigs (ACCs; n = 2,402) were annotated for mobile genetic elements (MGEs), biocide/metal resistance genes (BMRGs), virulence factor genes (VFGs), nitrogen-cycling genes (NCycGs), and putative host taxonomy. The resistomes exhibited substantial diversity (264 ARG subtypes) and spatial heterogeneity, with subtype richness in the Adyar (up to 171 subtypes) than in the Musi, where richness progressively declined downstream. Rank IV determinants dominated ARG abundance (77.82%), whereas Rank I determinants accounted for only 9.89%. MGEs were detected on just 3.12% (75/2,402) of ACCs, predominantly comprising plasmid-like contigs and proximal ARG-MGE associations. Co-occurrence with BMRGs was observed on 386 ACCs, whereas VFGs were uncommon (26 ACCs) and primarily represented dual-annotated efflux and envelope-integrity determinants rather than independent virulence loci. NCyc annotations were sparse (12 ACCs), with no evidence of complete nitrification or denitrification pathways. Taxonomic classification resolved 217 ACCs to the species level, with no matches to curated human pathogenic bacteria. Only two Acinetobacter-assigned ACCs exhibited both genus-level pathogenicity and mobility evidence. These findings highlight the importance of integrating mobility and host-taxonomic information to distinguish baseline environmental resistance from potential priorities for AMR surveillance.

papers.title: In situ single-cell CRISPR screens uncover context-dependent rewiring of glioma states and immune recruitment
papers.abstract: In vivo single-cell CRISPR screens can resolve perturbation effects in native tissues, but few combine cell-type-restricted delivery, somatic tumor initiation, and combinatorial perturbation. Here we developed an RCAS-TVA-based single-cell CRISPR screening approach coupling oncogenic transformation with single- or dual-guide perturbation in defined neural progenitors. In glioma, tumor suppressor loss produced distinct genotype-dependent transcriptional states, including an NF1-loss-associated increase in mesenchymal programs. Introducing a fixed Cdkn2a(ARF) perturbation altered malignant-cell state composition, immune-cell abundance, and the effects of additional tumor-suppressor perturbations, including increased representation of Pten- and Rb1-deficient cells, suggestive of the relief of an ARF-dependent genetic barrier. These perturbations converged on transcriptional states resembling pharmacologic p53 activation in human glioblastoma. Across mouse tumors and human glioblastoma models, this response was associated with increased astrocyte-like state representation. These findings establish a framework for single-cell analysis of context-dependent somatic perturbations during tumor initiation in vivo.

papers.title: Time-resolved single-cell screening reveals the dynamic regulatory architecture of human cardiogenesis
papers.abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) originates during early embryogenesis, yet when disease genes act cannot be determined from existing data. Human fetal heart atlases lack critical time points, and perturbation screens that systematically assess gene function currently profile at most a few time points. Here we combined single-cell CRISPR screening of 400 disease-relevant genes in cardioids, sampled daily over seven developmental days (~975,000 cells), with a matched multiome atlas. Perturbation phenotypes were strongly dependent on developmental stage. Perturbations that reshaped cell-fate allocation or gene expression were enriched for CHD-linked genes, and most acted already during progenitor stages. Timing was largely independent of the target gene's own expression, marking instead when a cell state became functionally dependent on it, and some effects persisted after expression declined. Consensus gene regulatory networks integrating perturbation and multiome data recovered stage-specific regulators and nominated HOXB2 and HOXB3 as candidate cardiac regulators. Many perturbations converged on shared downstream programmes, which were reorganised through differentiation. Effects correlated in progenitors were maintained in differentiated cells, split into distinct programmes, converged with other perturbations or disappeared entirely, indicating that gene function is highly context dependent. Beyond advancing our understanding of the developmental regulatory logic underlying CHD, our work provides a resource for developing context-dependent models for in silico prediction of perturbation effects.

papers.title: A Y-specific translocated gsdf copy is a candidate master sex-determining gene in common dab (Limanda limanda)
papers.abstract: Sex-determining systems in flatfishes are highly diverse, and even closely related species can differ in both sex-determining loci and heterogametic systems. In common dab (Limanda limanda), the genetic basis of sex determination has not yet been established. Here, we investigated sex determination using pooled whole-genome sequencing combined with long-read genome sequencing of females and males from Iceland and Norway. Genome-wide allele-frequency analyses identified sex-associated regions consistent with male heterogamety (XX/XY), with the strongest signal on chromosome 16. Comparison of the existing reference assembly, which represents an X haplotype at this locus, with a haplotype-resolved male PacBio HiFi assembly revealed a [~]21.5 kb Y-specific insertion on chromosome 16. The insertion showed complete coverage in male pools but little or no coverage in female pools from either population. It contained a translocated genomic segment including a copy of gonadal soma-derived factor (gsdf) and a predicted gene of unknown function. Comparative genomic analyses were consistent with this segment originating from an autosomal gsdf-containing region on chromosome 1. Given the recurrent recruitment of gsdf as a sex-determining factor in teleosts, we designate the Y-linked copy gsdfY and identify it as the strongest candidate for the master sex-determining gene in common dab. Additional broad sex-associated differentiation on chromosome 19 was restricted to the Icelandic samples and may reflect population-specific expansion of the sex-linked region, although its structural basis remains unresolved. Together, these findings provide the first genomic characterization of sex determination in common dab and demonstrate how gene duplication and translocation can contribute to the evolution of novel sex-determining systems in flatfishes.

papers.title: Genomes2Genes: A Progressive Cactus Gene Analysis Pipeline
papers.abstract: Whole-genome alignments are fundamental resources in comparative genomics, because they place genes and their surrounding sequences in a shared evolutionary context. Progressive Cactus aligns large numbers of genomes without a reference genome and reconstructs ancestral sequences along the input phylogeny. However, its Hierarchical Alignment Format output has mainly been used for visualization, phylogenomics, and pangenome studies, and gene-level analyses of these alignments remain difficult. Here, we present Genomes2Genes, a pipeline that converts Progressive Cactus graph-based alignments into validated coding sequence alignments of extant species and their reconstructed ancestors. The pipeline extracts exon alignment blocks, handles atypical genomic jumps, stitches exons into transcripts, and reports start codons, stop codons, and frameshifting indels across species, with validation steps throughout and a base-by-base audit of the final alignments. It catches both biological and technical artifacts and can be run on any part of the genome. We anticipate that this pipeline will be useful in identifying and removing problematic regions used in the potential reconstruction of species or gene phylogenies. We developed and tested the pipeline on a whole-genome alignment of 21 Brassicaceae species and 2 outgroups and found that, among 45,491 lineage-specific genes, the pipeline supported 22,376 candidate de novo genes, of which 1,811 had complete evidence of enabler mutations. Genomes2Genes is publicly available and extends whole-genome alignments to gene-level questions in comparative genomics and evolutionary biology.

papers.title: Telotrons: spliceosomal introns composed of telomeric repeats
papers.abstract: Spliceosomal intron numbers vary widely across eukaryotes, but the only established mechanism for large bursts of intron gain is the spread of transposable introner elements. We describe telotrons, spliceosomal introns composed predominantly of telomeric repeats. In a survey of 10,310 eukaryotic genome assemblies, we identified 7,008 introns with >85% telomeric repeat coverage and an additional 44,423 with >50% to [≤]85% coverage, in 25 genomes spanning haptophytes, dinoflagellates, a cryptophyte, stramenopiles, the apicomplexan Eimeria, and the nematode Mesorhabditis. Most telotrons carry GT-AG or GC-AG splice boundaries, and RNA-seq supports their splicing. Their repeat orientations are consistent with telomerase extension of broken DNA ends, and intron absence at corresponding positions in orthologs supports widespread de novo gain. In Eimeria and Mesorhabditis, telotrons instead occupy positions where orthologs carry ordinary introns, suggesting modification of existing introns. Telotrons thus point to telomerase as an endogenous driver of structural innovation through intron creation and remodeling.

papers.title: Lifestyle-mediated shifts in the gut microbiome and host genetics modulate gene expression in intestinal organoids
papers.abstract: Industrialization-associated shifts in the gut microbiome have been linked to disease, but the mechanisms by which microbial communities influence host gene regulation remain poorly understood. We developed a live microbiome-colonic organoid (colonoid) co-culture system to investigate genotype-dependent host responses to gut microbial community variation. Colonoid 2D monolayers from healthy donors were co-cultured with live gut microbial communities from individuals living urban or rural lifestyles, followed by RNA-sequencing. Urban and rural microbiomes elicited largely shared transcriptional responses, however they induced distinct host genetic effects on gene expression. We identified 511 host genes with microbiome-dependent allele-specific expression (ASE) which were involved in epithelial architecture, cell-matrix interactions and structural integrity. Notably, 149 host genes had distinct allelic effects between Urban and Rural microbiomes (urban-rural condition specific ASE or cASE), revealing genotype-dependent host responses to lifestyle-associated microbiomes. Urban-rural cASE was associated with microbial community composition, predominantly involving Prevotella and Bacteroides species. Targeted Prevotella copri spike-in recapitulated Prevotella-associated allelic effects at specific loci, including one in the IBD-associated autophagy gene, ATG4B. Together, these findings establish an experimental framework to investigate genotype-by-microbiome interactions, and demonstrate that lifestyle-mediated shifts in the microbiome modify host cis-regulatory genetic effects on gene expression.

papers.title: A population-scale isoform atlas enables isoform-based trait association and regulatory analysis in lettuce
papers.abstract: Genomic variation shapes phenotypic diversity, yet how genetic variation contributes to transcript isoform diversity remains poorly understood at the population scale. Here, we integrated transcriptomic data from 240 lettuce accessions with a lettuce pangenome to construct a comprehensive pan isoform atlas comprising 531,657 isoforms from 49,729 transcribed loci. Isoform presence absence variation (iPAV) captured extensive transcript diversification during domestication and horticultural differentiation, providing additional resolution beyond locus-level analyses, particularly within loci shared across the population. To facilitate the systematic analysis of isoform trait associations, we developed ISONET-GWAS, a computational framework that integrates isoform-based association mapping, functional annotation, and network-based candidate prioritization. ISONET-GWAS recovered the known chlorophyll regulator LsGLK, identified 455 metabolite isoform associations across 77 metabolites, and prioritized candidate regulators of chlorophyll metabolism supported by functional validation. Genome-wide splicing quantitative trait locus (sQTL) mapping identified 10,498 sQTL associations, revealing widespread distal genetic associations with alternative splicing and candidate trans-sQTL hotspots. Notably, we identified a trans-sQTL hotspot overlapping LsPPR, which encodes a pentatricopeptide repeat RNA-binding protein. Perturbation of LsPPR resulted in widespread changes in alternative splicing of floweing-related genes, accompanied by delayed bolting and flowering and altered splicing of flowering-related genes. Together, our study establishes a population-scale pan-isoform resource and a broadly applicable analytical strategy for isoform-level trait association, candidate prioritization, and complementary analysis of the genetic regulation of alternative splicing in crops.

papers.title: MaaD-TAD: an all-atom model of the duplicated PRAMEF/HNRNPCL chromatin domain built from sequence homology
papers.abstract: In the nucleus, the placement of genes in the 3D fold of DNA affects how they function. Models of this fold use two kinds of data: contact maps constructed from Hi-C, and nucleosome maps showing where DNA is wound around nucleosomes. Over evolution, sections of the genome were copied, creating near-identical regions. Reads from these regions cannot be assigned to one copy and are discarded, leaving "void regions" in both maps. We tested MaaD-TAD, a pipeline that models topologically associating domains (TADs) at the atomic level, on the PRAMEF/HNRNPCL locus on human chromosome 1. This challenging locus spans 652 kb, with only 15% of its nucleosome positions known and most contact data missing. To test our hypothesis that copies with similar sequence lie close in space, i.e. homology as a surrogate for proximity, we constructed a map of sequence homology in place of Hi-C and used CSynth to fold it into a 3D path. We then lengthened the path to fit a chromatin fibre, and refined the model by adding cohesin complexes, which stabilize chromatin structure. Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex through which a loop of chromatin is threaded; the loop is commonly anchored by CTCF proteins bound on either leg. Using known databases, we placed CTCF sites in our model and joined three to their copies with cohesin rings; in each pair the sites face each other, as loop anchors do. The final model holds 3,359 nucleosomes and about 55 million atoms. Micro-C, an advanced, higher-resolution form of Hi-C, provided data on two other duplicated regions that support our hypothesis: matching copies touched 1.2 to 1.9 times more often than expected. Our approach provides a novel method to reconstruct DNA regions with absent contact data and, to our knowledge, the first all-atom model of a complete TAD.

papers.title: Genomes of Solenogastres Shed Light on Ancestral Molluscan Biomineralization Genes
papers.abstract: Aplacophora (Solenogastres + Caudofoveata) is a group of worm-like molluscs that lack a shell and instead are covered with aragonitic spines and scales called sclerites. Sclerites are also found along the girdle in chitons (Polyplacophora) and are a synapomorphy for Aculifera (Aplacophora + Polyplacophora), which is the sister taxon of all other shell-bearing molluscs (Conchifera). However, whether the same genetic mechanism underlies the process of biomineralization in aculiferans and conchiferans is unknown. To investigate evolution of genes involved in biomineralization across Mollusca, we re-sequenced the genomes of two species of Solenogastres, Epimenia babai and Neomenia megatrapezata , producing near-chromosome-level assemblies through PacBio HiFi and Hi-C scaffolding. Using a combination of orthology inference and similarity searches against a known SMP database we identified 1,244 putative SMP orthogroups across Mollusca, 292 of which were present in at least one solenogaster genome. SMPs undergoing significant expansion/contraction at key nodes were further investigated. Of these, 15 were found in at least one solenogaster genome and included families containing chitin-binding, von Willebrand factor A, and C-type lectin domains. Across Mollusca, Solenogastres showed the highest number of significant losses in all gene families, including the SMPs investigated. Targeted searches for structural, silk-like proteins in Aculifera show further reductions in Solenogastres (16-17) compared to caudofoveates (29) and chitons (46-80). Altogether, our results support a conserved but reduced biomineralization toolkit underlying sclerite formation in Solenogastres and identify candidate genes for further proteomic and functional study.

papers.title: Systematic promoter perturbation reveals limitations of AlphaGenome gene expression predictions
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) models promise to facilitate the interpretation of noncoding variants by predicting their effects on gene regulation directly from genomic sequence. However, whether these models recapitulate fundamental principles of transcriptional biology remains unclear. Here, we tested whether AlphaGenome recognizes the expected consequences of promoter disruption on predicted gene expression. We systematically perturbed annotated promoter elements in silico for 2,111 promoter-gene pairs using dinucleotide shuffling, GC-adjusted random base substitution, and N-masking. We then compared AlphaGenome-predicted CAGE and RNA-sequencing signals across 20 tissues for reference and promoter-disrupted sequences. While CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions were strongly correlated for reference sequences, promoter disruption markedly reduced predicted CAGE activity, with N masking producing reductions of approximately three orders of magnitude. By contrast, the predicted RNA-sequencing signals were substantially less affected, resulting in an uncoupling of two molecular readouts of gene expression. Exon-level analyses showed that AlphaGenome predicted reduced RNA-sequencing signal when exonic sequences are within the disrupted region, but frequently failed to propagate this effect to downstream exons. This divergence between the CAGE and RNA-sequencing readouts was apparent from the second exon onward and was more pronounced in longer genes. Although alternative transcription initiation and shared downstream exons may explain individual cases, it is unlikely to account for the systematic discordance between CAGE and RNA-sequencing predictions. These findings indicate that AlphaGenome can recognize the local loss of promoter activity without consistently capturing its consequences across the corresponding transcript. More broadly, our results show that predictions from individual S2F output tracks do not necessarily reflect a coherent model of transcription. Systematic biological benchmarking and experimental validation therefore remain essential before such predictions can be used to prioritize or classify noncoding variants in research or diagnostic settings.

papers.title: Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis Reveals Differential Exon Usage and Virulence Gene Family Dynamics in Plasmodium falciparum during Severe Malaria
papers.abstract: Malaria remains a leading cause of child mortality in developing countries, with roughly 610,000 deaths per year. While the disease is caused by five human Plasmodium species, Plasmodium falciparum (Pf ) causes the most severe form. Progression from uncomplicated to severe malaria is characterized by high proliferation of the parasite, severely affecting children under five years old. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying disease progression remain an active area of research. Many multicopy genes have been implicated in Pf virulence. Some of these genes are implicated in cytoadherence, host-cell invasion, immune evasion, sequestration of infected erythrocytes, and antigenic variation. We employed an integrative transcriptomic analysis in this study to elucidate the molecular underpinnings of severe malaria and gene expression patterns, virulence gene dynamics, and the potential contribution of alternative splicing. Results show an overexpression of protein synthesis and ribosomal genes associated with severe malaria. About 86% (n=1865) of all differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were downregulated in severe malaria, and 226 genes exhibited both differential expression and differential exon usage (DEU). Pf virulence genes and antigenic genes such as var (pfEMP1), stevor, surfin, rif (rifin), ptm-2TM, and msp were upregulated in severe malaria compared with uncomplicated malaria, except for rifin. In severe malaria, there was evidence of co-expression and regulation within multigene families, as well as DEU and alternative splicing in virulence genes and antimalarial resistance-related proteins. Pf does not employ a single mechanism for disease progression but suppresses and deregulates nonessential pathways, processes, and genes, which are upregulated virulence genes, DNA replication, mRNA transcription, and protein synthesis. Multicopy genes are co-expressed and regulated to meet the molecular needs of the parasite. The parasite employs alternative splicing and DEU mechanisms for immune invasion and evasion, host-parasite interaction, as well as antimalarial resistance.

papers.title: Population Genomics of the Bovine Sialic Acid Network Reveals Functional and Evolutionary Diversity Across European and South African Cattle Breeds
papers.abstract: **Background:** Sialic acids, mainly N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac) and N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), are terminal monosaccharides of glycans involved in numerous physiological processes, such as immune and neuronal function. Their biosynthesis, transport, transfer and turnover depend on a network of genes, but genetic studies in cattle have mostly addressed individual genes or genetic associations with milk oligosaccharide concentrations, leaving variation across this network largely uncharacterized. In bovine milk, sialylated glycans that depend on this network vary among animals and change rapidly during early lactation. We therefore characterized variation in 13 selected genes of the bovine sialic acid network using whole-genome sequence data from European and South African cattle. **Results:** We analyzed 346 animals from 12 European and 4 South African breeds. Of 9,724 variants in the 13 target genes, 8,675 were intronic and 62 were predicted to alter the amino acid sequence. Integration of SIFT predictions, Rate4Site conservation and protein context, with population representation as supporting evidence, identified 15 prioritized candidates, including 7 high-priority candidates in NEU3, ST8SIA2, ST8SIA4, CMAH and ST3GAL4. The most differentiated candidates were not among the 15 prioritized variants. NEU3 Y136H showed the largest regional contrast in allele frequency (0.83 in South African and 0.34 in European cattle), whereas several prioritized candidates were represented by a single allele in the South African cohort. Genome-wide principal component analysis of 950,219 linkage-disequilibrium-pruned SNPs separated South African from European cattle along the first component, which explained about 25% of the variance. None of the 220 analyzed common pathway SNPs exceeded the corresponding genome-wide differentiation thresholds at breed, country or regional level. Within the ascertained pathway SNPs, diversity was higher in South African breeds, and Tajima's D was shifted toward positive values in European breeds and centered near zero in South African breeds. **Conclusions:** This study provides a network-wide map of predicted protein-altering variation in the bovine sialic acid pathway and identifies 15 candidates for functional investigation, most of them rare. Because the most differentiated variants were not those with the strongest functional support, population contrasts, evolutionary conservation and protein context provide complementary evidence for selecting candidates. The analyzed common pathway SNPs did not show exceptional differentiation relative to the genome-wide background. The candidates provide specific targets for genotyping, enzyme-level testing and genotype-informed milk phenotyping.

papers.title: Integrating bacterial genomics and host transcriptomics links Burkholderia pseudomallei variation to melioidosis mortality and neutrophil responses
papers.abstract: Bacterial genetic variation contributes to the outcome of infection, but its relationship with host immune responses is rarely investigated in the same patients, limiting the biological interpretation of pathogen-associated disease severity. Here, we integrated pathogen genomics, clinical outcomes and host transcriptomics to investigate host-pathogen interactions in melioidosis, a frequently fatal infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. We analysed prospective clinical data from 2,142 patients, whole-genome sequences from 2,101 infecting isolates and 646 paired host blood transcriptomes across five cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. Infections were typically dominated by a single strain, with limited within-host diversification, supporting the use of an infecting isolate genome to investigate pathogen-associated clinical outcomes. Bacterial genome-wide association studies identified one locus associated with binary mortality at genome-wide significance. Incorporating patient age, sex, body mass index and Charlson Comorbidity Index increased this to four, while modelling time to death as a continuous phenotype identified seven loci. Integration with paired host transcriptomes linked mortality-associated bacterial genetic variation to imputed signatures of increased immature neutrophils and reduced neutrophil degranulation. An intergenic region upstream of the polyketide synthesis locus BPSS1006-BPSS1011 was additionally associated with downregulation of host genes involved in myeloid-cell signalling and cell proliferation pathways. These findings connect naturally occurring B. pseudomallei genomic variation associated with mortality to distinct host immune signatures, providing insight into pathogen-host interactions underlying severe melioidosis and a framework for investigating the contribution of pathogen genetic diversity to clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Personalised Gene Expression Prediction Improves Cell-Type-Specific Association Testing
papers.abstract: Linking genetic variation to disease requires accurate prediction of its effects on gene expression in relevant cell types. Sequence-to-function models offer a way to predict these effects and, with training on personal genomes, have begun to capture inter-individual expression differences. However, effect sign accuracy remains limited, and predictive uncertainty is unquantified. Here we introduce ATTICUS, which combines personalised sequence representations with uncertainty-aware expression prediction. ATTICUS transfers regulatory information learned in bulk expression pretraining to cell-type-specific expression prediction without requiring genotypes paired with single-cell expression data. Across blood and brain cell types in OneK1K and ROSMAP, ATTICUS approximately doubles expression prediction correlations relative to scPrediXcan and substantially improves sign accuracy. Moreover, ATTICUS enables uncertainty-aware transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). Applied to systemic lupus erythematosus and Alzheimer's disease, ATTICUS identifies more associations, with greater cell-type specificity and stronger directional concordance, and reduced statistical inflation. Together, our results demonstrate that personalised training makes predictions more directionally consistent, and uncertainty propagation improves the calibration of TWAS and the prioritisation of disease genes. ATTICUS provides a framework for both, enabling the use of single-cell expression datasets without matched genotypes to inform uncertainty-aware TWAS, expanding their use in prioritising disease-associated genes and cell types.

papers.title: Transcriptome profiling reveals gene regulatory network governing seed size in Brassica napus
papers.abstract: Seed size is a critical trait influencing yield and quality in oilseed crops such as Brassica napus. Despite their economic importance, the genetic and molecular mechanisms regulating seed size remain unclear, particularly in polyploid species, such as B. napus. To deepen our understanding of seed size regulation, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis across four developmental stages (heart, torpedo, green, and mature) and three distinct seed organs: the seed coat, embryo, and endosperm. Differential expression analysis between B. napus var. Zhongshuang (ZS11) and B. napus cv. Ragged Jack (RJ) was performed to uncover regulatory networks involved in seed size control. Our results uncovered dynamic gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and pinpointed key regulators, including well-established factors like ABI5 and BRI1, as well as novel candidate genes such as KNAT5, ARF11, SUS2, UGT72B1, UGT89A2, and SBT1.7. The present research provides an understanding of the regulatory networks governing seed size in B. napus. These findings not only enhance our knowledge of seed biology but also offer valuable resources for future breeding strategies aimed at optimizing seed size and yield in polyploid oilseed crops.

papers.title: Segment-dependent phylogenetic resolution reveals geographic and host sampling gaps in Oropouche virus genomes
papers.abstract: Background. Oropouche virus (OROV) has been reported in areas beyond its historical Amazonian range since 2023, accompanied by rapid growth in publicly available genomic data. However, the extent to which these data provide reliable phylogenetic and epidemiological resolution, and whether that resolution differs among genome segments, has not been systematically examined. Methods. Nucleotide sequences annotated under Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense were retrieved from NCBI Virus (accessed 13 May 2025) and filtered to retain records at least 70% of the reference length for each segment, yielding 898 S, 831 M, and 832 L sequences. Segments were aligned independently with MAFFT, and maximum-likelihood phylogenies were inferred with IQ-TREE using ModelFinder and ultrafast bootstrap approximation. Trees were annotated with collection date, country, and host in iTOL. Results. Phylogenetic resolution differed among segments. Contemporary Brazilian sequences formed a largely unresolved region in the S segment tree, whereas the M and L trees resolved recent clusters to differing degrees. Resolution did not track segment length: the M tree resolved contemporary structure more strongly than the longer L tree, and total tree length was approximately 3.5 times greater in the M tree despite near-identical taxon sampling. Sequences collected before 2010 were recovered in supported clusters in all three segment trees, although their configuration differed by segment. These sequences were also predominantly non-Brazilian and non-human, preventing collection date, geographic origin, and host from being separated as explanations for the observed clustering. The species-level query also retained three reassortant viruses, which may influence segment-specific topologies; sequences annotated to the United States were Iquitos virus rather than OROV. Two Italian sequences clustered with Cuban sequences across all three trees, concordant with published travel histories. Conclusions. Publicly available sequences contain phylogenetic structure that differs among the S, M, and L segment trees, but interpretation is constrained by uneven temporal, geographic, and host sampling and by the inclusion of reassortant species in a species-level dataset. The concentration of sequences from Brazil and human hosts, together with limited representation of non-human hosts, restricts inference about OROV diversity and ecology. Broader and more balanced genomic surveillance would improve the ability to resolve OROV evolutionary and transmission patterns.

papers.title: Mutation and Recombination Rates in Free-Ranging Polar Bears
papers.abstract: Mutation rate () and recombination rate (r) are fundamental population-genetic parameters, yet demographic and conservation inference in polar bears (Ursus maritimus) has relied on values borrowed from humans and other mammals. Known values vary by an order of magnitude across mammals, and inaccuracies in these estimates propagate into downstream analyses, such as inferences of demographic history. To address this, we used high-coverage whole-genome resequencing of eight parent-offspring trios from the Western Hudson Bay subpopulation of polar bears. We identified 329 de novo mutations and estimated a pedigree-based germline mutation rate of 1.22 x 10?? per site per generation, which is within the mammalian range and close to values previously assumed for this species. Trio-based phasing yielded 522 crossovers across 16 meioses (32.6 per meiosis), and a pedigree-inferred recombination rate of 1.50 cM/Mb. From 44 unrelated individuals sampled from the same subpopulation, we inferred a demography-aware recombination map with a length-weighted genome-wide recombination rate of 3.03 cM/Mb (median 1.28 cM/Mb). We also identified 8,515 recombination hotspot regions covering 2.10% of the genome, accounting for 43.8% of total map length, a 20.9-fold concentration. Crossovers overlapped LD-defined hotspots 5.06-fold more often than expected by chance (p < 0.001). Nucleotide diversity was low and positively rank-correlated with recombination rate, consistent with linked selection. Genomic features explained only ~3% of recombination rate variation, with GC content and SINE abundance the only significant predictors. These species-specific parameters provide an empirical foundation for future demographic reconstruction and population projection in this vulnerable, ice-obligate species.

papers.title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica) reveals extensive centromeric satellite arrays
papers.abstract: We present a chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly from Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica). The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes of 322 Mb and 295 Mb, with 89.7% and 95.6% respectively, each scaffolded into 7 chromosomes. Assembly completeness is high (BUSCO 97.8% in each haplotype), with 34,213 and 29,684 annotated protein-coding genes for haplotypes one and two, respectively. The chromosomes contain extensive centromeric satellite arrays that cover up to half of some chromosomes. Their precise functional boundaries remain undetermined.
